name: SSC CGL
fullName: Staff Selection Commission – Combined Graduate Level Examination
approxCandidates: ≈28 lakh registered for Tier 1 (2026 cycle, as reported)
eligibility: Bachelor's degree from a recognised university; 18–32 years (post-wise upper limits, with category relaxations)

notification.summary: CGL 2026 was notified on 21 May 2026 (≈10,731 tentative vacancies after revision, as reported; the original notice was reported at ≈12,256). Tier 1 CBT is under way from 30 Sep 2026 to late Oct 2026 with sectional timing introduced this year; Tier 2 is expected in December 2026.

importantDates.date: From 27 Sep 2026, 2–3 days before each shift

pattern.notes: Tier 1 is qualifying; merit is on Tier 2. From the 2026 cycle each section reportedly has its own 15-minute timer (no switching between sections). Scores are normalised across shifts. 80 minutes for scribe-eligible candidates.

trendAnalysis.summary: Tier 1 has been moderate overall, with Quant the toughest and most time-consuming section (algebra identities, geometry and trigonometry carry ~30% of it) and Reasoning the most scoring. Reasoning is dominated by analogy, classification, series, coding and number puzzles, plus 4–6 non-verbal figures. General Awareness leans on static GK – history, polity, geography and science – with 2–4 current-affairs questions and a growing share of art & culture. English is vocabulary-heavy (synonyms, idioms, one-word substitution, spelling) with one cloze passage and one reading passage. The 2026 cycle adds sectional timing, which rewards balanced speed across all four sections.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from the commission's published question-paper/response-sheet format and from shift-wise memory-based papers and topic-wise analyses published by coaching sites (Testbook, Adda247, PW, Careers360 day-wise analyses) for the 2023–2025 cycles, cross-checked against the writer's own knowledge of SSC papers. Live web fetches during this round returned only summary pages (SSC barred public discussion of 2025 papers), so question-type detail relies mainly on prior knowledge of the papers; frequencies are approximate per-shift counts. Figure-based (non-verbal) archetypes are recorded but only text-renderable variants are used for generated questions.

archetypes.pattern: Word-pair analogy (A : B :: C : ?) built on a semantic relation – worker : tool, product : raw material, organ : function, instrument : quantity measured, young one : animal; distractors are words of the same category that do not share the relation.

Number-pair/triad analogy where the second term comes from an arithmetic rule on the first (n² ± k, n³ ± k, ×k ± c, digit operations); often framed with two example pairs and a note to operate on whole numbers without splitting digits; distractors satisfy the rule for only one pair or come from ±1 slips.
Letter-cluster analogy (ABCD : EFGH :: ? ) where each letter moves by a fixed or alternating +/− shift or is replaced by its opposite letter (A↔Z); distractors differ in exactly one letter.
Odd-one-out among four words/objects by category or property (three belong to one class, e.g. instruments, organs, rivers of one state); the trap is a surface feature shared by the odd item.
Odd number / number-pair / triad out of four where three follow one arithmetic rule (squares, primes, (a, b, c) with c = a×b − k, divisibility); the odd option breaks the rule by a small margin.
Odd letter-cluster out of four where three clusters have the same positional gaps (e.g. +2, +3 or opposite-letter pairs) and one breaks the gap pattern.
Number series with one missing/next term following a two-step rule (×k + c, alternating operations, differences forming squares/primes or their own series).

Letter or alphanumeric cluster series (e.g. three-letter groups with each position advancing by its own increment, possibly mixed with numbers); find the next cluster; distractors shift one position wrongly.
Word → letter code by a positional rule (each letter shifted by +k/−k, alternate shifts, reversal then shift, or opposite letters); decode the rule from one example and encode a new word.

Word → number code from alphabet positions (sum of positions, sum × k, sum of reverse positions, number of letters × k); apply the rule to a new word; distractors use forward instead of reverse positions.
Sentence coding: two or three short sentences coded as groups of code words; identify the code of a given word by finding the common word/code between statements.
Verbal chain / introduction ('pointing to a photo…') blood relation: trace 3–4 links and name the relation; traps are gender assumptions and the paternal/maternal side.
Coded blood relations: symbols (A + B, A × B, A − B …) stand for relations; decode an expression to find how two people are related, or which expression makes a given relation true.

Walking path of 3–5 legs with left/right turns; find the shortest distance and/or direction from the start (often a Pythagorean triple); or the final facing direction after a sequence of left/right/clockwise turns; traps are direction after a 'right turn' and adding instead of subtracting legs.
Two/three statements ('All/Some/No') with two conclusions; decide which follow, including 'Some … are not' and possibility-type conclusions; trap is reversing 'All A are B'.
Symbol substitution: '+' means '×', '−' means '÷' etc.; rewrite and evaluate an expression with BODMAS; distractors come from left-to-right evaluation.
Which two signs (or two numbers) must be interchanged to make a given equation correct; each option names a pair of signs to swap.
Missing term inside a number sequence (often the middle term) built from a mixed rule such as ×1 + 1, ×2 + 2, ×3 + 3 … or alternating × and +; find the term that replaces '?'.
Defined-operation missing number: from two or three solved examples (a ★ b = …) infer the rule (a² + b², (a + b)², a×b + a …) and apply it; distractors fit just one example.
Number grid / figure (given as rows): each row or column follows the same rule (e.g. third = first × second − k, or sum of squares); find the missing number.

Position from both ends: total in a row/class from two ranks, rank from the other end, persons between two people, or a short comparison chain (taller/older) to find who is at a rank; trap is ±1 counting.
Arrange 5 words in dictionary order (common prefix, differing late letters) or find which word comes at a given position.
Calendar: day of the week for a date given a reference date (odd-days counting across leap years) or after n days.
Clock angle between the hands at a given time (30H − 5.5M) or time when hands coincide/are opposite.
Overlapping groups described as counts in each region of a three-circle Venn diagram; find how many belong to an exact combination (e.g. both A and B but not C).
Choose the description of the Venn diagram that best represents three classes (one inside another, partial overlap, disjoint).
Linear or circular seating of 5–7 persons with 4–6 clues (immediate neighbour, 'second to the left', ends); question asks who sits at a position or between two people.
Mirror image of a clock time or of an alphanumeric/number string (vertical mirror on the right); time question solved by 11:60 − time.
A square sheet is folded once or twice and punched/cut; predict how it looks (number/position of holes) when unfolded.
Count triangles/squares in a figure built from a square or triangle with diagonals and mid-lines.
Dice: from two or three positions of the same die, find the face opposite to a given face; or a painted cube cut into n³ small cubes – count cubes with 0/1/2/3 painted faces.

Ancient and medieval India: dynasty founders, capitals, rulers' titles, Buddhist/Jain councils, Delhi Sultanate/Mughal/Vijayanagara rulers, battles with years and administrative reforms; distractors are rulers of the same or adjacent dynasty.
Modern India and freedom struggle: founders of organisations/newspapers, INC sessions and presidents, movements with years, Governors-General and their acts.
Article-number question: which Article deals with a given provision (FR, DPSP, office, emergency, finance); distractors are nearby Article numbers.
Constitution-making, Preamble, amendments, schedules and parts with their subject matter (e.g. which Schedule/amendment added X); distractors are adjacent schedules/amendments.
Constitutional/statutory offices: appointment, qualification (age), tenure, removal, oath, and borrowed features of the Constitution.
Indian physical geography: rivers (origin, tributaries, states), lakes, passes, hills, national parks and their states.
Soils, crops, minerals, climate and resources of India (which soil/crop/mineral/region; seasons and winds).
World/physical geography: atmosphere layers, ocean currents, straits, planets, latitudes and landforms.
Banking and monetary policy: RBI instruments (repo, CRR, SLR), functions, institutions and their headquarters.
Economic concepts and planning: GDP/GNP, deficits, inflation measures, Five-Year Plans, taxes, government schemes and their launch.
Physics: SI units and instruments, and everyday phenomena (mirrors/lenses, dispersion, sound speed, heat, electricity).
Chemistry: common names/formulae of compounds, ores and alloys, acids in foods, pH, gases and periodic-table facts.
Human biology: vitamins/minerals and deficiency diseases, organs and glands, blood, diseases and their causative agents.
Plant biology and classification: tissues, photosynthesis, plant hormones, cell organelles, scientists behind classification.
Performing arts and festivals: classical/folk dances, festivals and fairs with their states, instruments and their maestros.
Temples, monuments and architectural styles with their builders/dynasties and locations.
Recent national/international events of the last 1–2 years: summits and hosts, missions, schemes and major appointments.
Sports: number of players, terms and trophies of a sport, venues, and recent Olympic/Asian Games/World Cup results involving India.
Book–author matching (classical and contemporary, including autobiographies) and literary/national award facts.
Unit digit of a power/product or remainder of a large power on division (cyclicity); distractors are adjacent cycle values.
Divisibility and number properties: smallest digit/number to add or subtract for divisibility by 9, 11, 8, which number is divisible, count of factors, primes, or sum of numbers in a range.
BODMAS simplification with fractions/decimals/brackets or 'value of ?' equations; distractors come from wrong operation order.
Basic/successive percentage: x% of a number, net effect of successive increases/decreases, or price rise vs consumption cut.
Percentage word problems: election votes, pass-fail marks, salary spent/saved; find the total or the difference.
Marked price above cost with a discount (or successive discounts) – find profit % or marked price.
Cost/selling price relation: profit % from CP and SP, CP from SP and gain %, CP of x items = SP of y items, two articles sold at the same price, or false-weight dealers.
Simple interest: find rate/time/principal from amounts, or the time to become n times.
Compound interest for 2–3 years, CI − SI difference, or half-yearly compounding.
Divide an amount in a given (sometimes fractional) ratio, or find shares/partnership profit.
Ratio change: number added/subtracted to change a ratio, combined ratio A : B : C, or mean/third proportional.
Average: simple or consecutive-number averages, inclusion/exclusion/replacement of a member (teacher's age, wrong entry corrected), or overlap of first-k and last-k averages.
Two/three workers with individual days; together, one leaves after some days, or efficiency ratio problems.
Pipes and cisterns (filling and emptying pipes together) or men-days (M₁D₁ = M₂D₂) proportionality.
Trains crossing a pole/platform/another train (same or opposite direction) with km/h ↔ m/s conversion.
Average speed for to-and-fro journeys, relative speed/chase problems, or boats and streams.
Reciprocal identities: given x ± 1/x = k, find x² + 1/x², x³ ± 1/x³ or x⁴ + 1/x⁴; distractors from sign slips.
Symmetric identities in a, b, c: (a + b + c)², a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc, or a + b + c = 0 shortcuts; also surds like (√a ± √b).
Triangle properties: angle at incentre/orthocentre, angle-bisector/median length, similarity ratios, Pythagorean right-triangle facts.
Circle theorems: chords intersecting, tangent length, angle in a semicircle, cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles.
Polygons and lines: interior/exterior angles, number of sides or diagonals, angles of a triangle with given ratios.
2-D mensuration: area/perimeter of rectangles, triangles (Heron's), circles and sectors, change in area with change in dimensions.
3-D mensuration: volume/surface area of cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere/hemisphere; melting and recasting.
Standard-angle values and identity simplification (sin²θ + cos²θ, complementary angles like tan 10° tan 80°).
Conditional trigonometry: given sec θ + tan θ, tan θ = a/b or similar, find another ratio/expression.
Small table/bar data (given in text) for 4–6 years or items: ratio, percentage increase, average or difference between categories.
Factual RC question on a 150–250-word passage: answer is stated in the passage; distractors use passage words with altered meaning.
Inference/main-idea/title RC question: choose the central theme or what the author implies.
Vocabulary/tone in context: synonym/antonym of a word used in the passage or the author's tone.
Cloze passage with five numbered blanks; each item tests contextual vocabulary, a connector or a preposition; distractors are near-synonyms that fail the collocation.
Single-sentence blank requiring the contextually correct word (collocation, near-synonym choice).
Single-sentence blank testing grammar – prepositions, articles, tense, conjunctions.
Synonym of a standalone or underlined word (moderate CGL-level vocabulary); distractors include antonyms and look-alike words.
Antonym of a standalone or underlined word; the trap option is a synonym of the given word.
Meaning of a common idiom/phrase (or the idiom that fits a sentence); distractors are literal readings.
One-word substitute for a descriptive phrase (persons, -cide, -phobia, -archy words); distractors are related words of the same family.
Select the correctly (or incorrectly) spelt word among four look-alike spellings (double letters, ie/ei, -ance/-ence).
Sentence split into 3–4 segments; error in subject–verb agreement, pronoun or noun number (each/one of/neither…nor, uncountable nouns).
Sentence split into segments; error in tense sequence, preposition, comparative/superlative, or conjunction pairs (hardly…when, no sooner…than).
Improve the bracketed/underlined part: tense, conditional, preposition or idiom usage; 'No improvement' sometimes an option.
Change active to passive (or vice versa) across tenses, including questions and modals; distractors change the tense.
Direct ↔ indirect speech: reporting verb change, backshift of tense, pronoun and time-word changes; imperatives with 'ordered/requested'.

resources.notes: SSC does not publish full question papers as PDFs. After each Tier, it releases tentative answer keys with each candidate's question paper and response sheet on ssc.gov.in (Answer Key section) for a limited window; final keys follow the result. Coaching sites compile shift-wise memory-based papers.

questions.question:
Select the letter-cluster that is related to the third cluster in the same way as the second is related to the first.
DFHJ : WUSQ :: KMOQ : ?
questions.explanation: Each letter is replaced by its opposite letter (positions add up to 27): D↔W, F↔U, H↔S, J↔Q. So K→P, M→N, O→L, Q→J, giving PNLJ.

relevance.note: Opposite-letter (A↔Z) cluster analogy exactly as set in CGL 2023-24; distractors differ by one letter

questions.question:
Select the number that will come in place of the question mark (?) in the series.
5, 11, 24, 51, 106, ?

relevance.note: ×2+1,×2+2… series with ±1-slip options, a staple CGL Tier-1 series

questions.question:
Select the term that will come next in the series.
AZ, CX, FU, JQ, ?
questions.explanation: First letters: A, C, F, J (+2, +3, +4) → next +5 = O. Second letters: Z, X, U, Q (−2, −3, −4) → next −5 = L. Answer: OL.

relevance.note: Two-letter cluster with +2..+5 / −2..−5 progression; matches CGL letter-series style

questions.question: In a certain code language, 'TABLE' is written as 'GZYOV'. How will 'CHAIR' be written in that language?
questions.explanation: Each letter is replaced by its opposite letter (A↔Z, B↔Y …): T→G, A→Z, B→Y, L→O, E→V. So C→X, H→S, A→Z, I→R, R→I = XSZRI.

relevance.note: Opposite-letter word coding (TABLE→GZYOV) is a recurring CGL coding type; trap option swaps last two letters

questions.question: In a certain code language, 'PAINT' is written as 'UOJBQ'. How will 'BRUSH' be written in that language?
questions.explanation: The word is reversed and each letter is moved one step forward: PAINT → TNIAP → UOJBQ. BRUSH → HSURB → ITVSC.

relevance.note: Reverse-then-+1 coding, frequent in CGL 2023-24; distractors from missing reversal

questions.question: Ravi walks 10 m towards North, turns right and walks 6 m, turns right again and walks 18 m, and then turns right and walks 6 m. How far and in which direction is he from his starting point?
questions.explanation: Take start (0, 0). North 10 → (0, 10); right = East 6 → (6, 10); right = South 18 → (6, −8); right = West 6 → (0, −8). He is 8 m South of the start.

relevance.note: Four-leg right-turn walk with net-displacement, standard CGL direction item

questions.question:
Statements:
Some cats are dogs.
No dog is a rat.
Conclusions:
I. Some cats are not rats.
II. No cat is a rat.
Which conclusion(s) follow(s)?
questions.explanation: The cats that are dogs cannot be rats, so 'Some cats are not rats' is certain. Other cats may or may not be rats, so II does not follow.

relevance.note: Some-cats/no-dog syllogism with 'some not' conclusion; classic CGL two-conclusion format

questions.question:
If '+' means '×', '−' means '+', '×' means '÷' and '÷' means '−', what is the value of:
16 × 4 + 3 − 8 ÷ 5

relevance.note: Sign-substitution BODMAS evaluation exactly as in CGL shifts

questions.question:
Arrange the following words in the order in which they appear in an English dictionary.
1. Plant  2. Planet  3. Plane  4. Planner  5. Plank
questions.explanation: Plane comes before Planet (it is its prefix). Then compare the 5th letters: Plan-e(t), Plan-k, Plan-n, Plan-t → Planet, Plank, Planner, Plant. Order: Plane, Planet, Plank, Planner, Plant = 3, 2, 5, 4, 1.

relevance.note: Five plan- words with late-letter differences, faithful CGL dictionary-order item

questions.question: If 15 August 2024 was a Thursday, what day of the week was 15 August 2026?
questions.explanation: From 15 Aug 2024 to 15 Aug 2025 there is no 29 February, so +1 day (Friday). From 15 Aug 2025 to 15 Aug 2026 there is again no 29 February, so +1 day → Saturday.

relevance.note: Odd-days across a non-leap year pair; CGL calendar type though labelled hard it is medium

questions.question: Who founded the Servants of India Society in 1905?
questions.explanation: Gopal Krishna Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society in Pune in 1905.

relevance.note: Founder of Servants of India Society 1905 is a typical CGL modern-history organisation question

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India lays down the procedure for the impeachment of the President?
questions.explanation: Article 61 deals with impeachment of the President. Article 72 is the pardoning power, Article 56 the term of office and Article 74 the Council of Ministers.

relevance.note: Article 61 impeachment with nearby-Article distractors, typical CGL article-number item

questions.question: Provisions relating to disqualification on the ground of defection (anti-defection law) are contained in which Schedule of the Constitution?
questions.explanation: The Tenth Schedule was added by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985 and deals with anti-defection.

relevance.note: Tenth Schedule anti-defection with adjacent-schedule distractors; CGL polity style

questions.question: Which river is popularly known as the 'Dakshin Ganga'?
questions.explanation: The Godavari, the longest river of peninsular India, is called the Dakshin Ganga (Ganga of the South).

relevance.note: 'Dakshin Ganga' epithet question appears in SSC papers; good river-nickname item

questions.question: Who is the chairperson of the GST Council?
options: Governor of the Reserve Bank of India
questions.explanation: Under Article 279A, the GST Council is chaired by the Union Finance Minister; state finance ministers are members.

relevance.note: GST Council chair asked in CGL economy sections; plausible office distractors

questions.question: The 'repo rate' is the rate at which:
options: commercial banks lend to their most creditworthy customers
the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities
the RBI borrows money from commercial banks
the government borrows from the public through bonds
questions.explanation: Repo (repurchase) rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against eligible securities. The rate at which the RBI absorbs funds from banks is the reverse repo / SDF rate.

relevance.note: Repo-rate definition with RBI-borrows reverse-repo trap; CGL banking style

questions.question: The Konark Sun Temple in Odisha was built during the reign of which ruler?
questions.explanation: The Konark Sun Temple (13th century) was built by King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

relevance.note: Konark–Narasimhadeva I (Eastern Ganga) matches CGL temple–builder questions

questions.question: What is the unit digit of 7³⁵?
questions.explanation: Unit digits of powers of 7 repeat in the cycle 7, 9, 3, 1. 35 = 4 × 8 + 3, so the unit digit is the 3rd in the cycle = 3.

relevance.note: Unit digit of 7^35 via cyclicity; standard CGL number-system item

questions.question: A shopkeeper marks an article 40% above its cost price and then allows a discount of 15% on the marked price. What is his profit percentage?

relevance.note: MP 40% above CP with 15% discount; classic CGL profit item with 25% trap

questions.question: What is the difference between the compound interest (compounded annually) and the simple interest on ₹12,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum?

relevance.note: CI−SI for 2 years via Pr²/100²; standard CGL formula item

questions.question: ₹7,800 is divided among A, B and C in the ratio 1/2 : 1/3 : 1/4. What is B's share?

relevance.note: Fractional-ratio division (1/2:1/3:1/4) exactly as CGL sets it

questions.question: The average of 11 numbers is 50. The average of the first six numbers is 49 and that of the last six numbers is 52. What is the sixth number?
questions.explanation: Sum of all = 550. First six = 294, last six = 312. The 6th number is counted twice: 294 + 312 − 550 = 56.

relevance.note: Overlapping 6th number average; a recurring CGL average type

questions.question: A can complete a work in 12 days and B in 18 days. They work together for 4 days, after which A leaves. In how many more days will B finish the remaining work?
questions.explanation: Together per day = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36. In 4 days = 20/36 = 5/9. Remaining 4/9 is done by B in (4/9) × 18 = 8 days.

relevance.note: A leaves after 4 days, B finishes; standard CGL time & work

questions.question: If x + 1/x = 5, what is the value of x³ + 1/x³?

relevance.note: x+1/x=5 → x³+1/x³ with 125 trap; textbook CGL algebra

questions.question: If a + b + c = 12 and a² + b² + c² = 50, what is the value of ab + bc + ca?
questions.explanation: (a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2(ab + bc + ca) → 144 = 50 + 2S → S = 47.

relevance.note: ab+bc+ca from sum and sum of squares; CGL identity item, 94 trap for not halving

questions.question: In triangle ABC, the bisectors of the interior angles B and C meet at O. If ∠A = 70°, what is ∠BOC?

relevance.note: ∠BOC = 90+A/2 incentre angle; very frequent in CGL geometry

questions.question: If sec θ + tan θ = 3, what is the value of sin θ?
questions.explanation: Since sec²θ − tan²θ = 1, sec θ − tan θ = 1/3. Adding: 2 sec θ = 10/3 → sec θ = 5/3; tan θ = 4/3. sin θ = tan θ / sec θ = 4/5.

relevance.note: sec+tan=3 → sin θ via reciprocal trick; classic CGL conditional trig

questions.question: Sales of a company (in ₹ crore): 2021 – 120, 2022 – 150, 2023 – 135, 2024 – 180, 2025 – 210. What is the average sales of those years in which sales were above the five-year average?

relevance.note: Text-table DI with above-average filter; matches CGL tabular DI computations

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.
FRUGAL
questions.explanation: Frugal means economical/sparing; its opposite is extravagant. Thrifty is a synonym.

relevance.note: FRUGAL antonym with Thrifty synonym trap; CGL-level word

questions.question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given phrase.
A person who is unable to pay his debts
questions.explanation: Insolvent = unable to pay debts. Inept = unskilled; impudent = disrespectful.

relevance.note: Insolvent OWS with In- prefix look-alikes; CGL style

questions.question: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling has double 'c' and double 'm': accommodate.

relevance.note: Accommodate double-c/double-m spelling, frequent in CGL

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.
Neither the manager / nor his assistants / was present / at the meeting.
questions.explanation: With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Assistants' is plural, so 'was' should be 'were'.

relevance.note: Neither…nor proximity agreement error; exact CGL error-spotting type

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error, or 'No error'.
Hardly had I / reached the station / than the train left.
questions.explanation: 'Hardly' is followed by 'when', not 'than': Hardly had I reached the station when the train left.

relevance.note: Hardly…than → when correlative error; recurring CGL item

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the underlined part of the sentence.
[If I was] the Prime Minister, I would ban single-use plastic.
questions.explanation: For an imaginary/hypothetical present condition, the subjunctive 'were' is used: If I were the Prime Minister…

relevance.note: Subjunctive 'If I were' improvement; common in CGL

questions.question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The committee has approved the proposal.
options: The proposal was approved by the committee.
The proposal had been approved by the committee.
The proposal has been approved by the committee.
The proposal is approved by the committee.
questions.explanation: Present perfect active (has approved) becomes present perfect passive (has been approved).

relevance.note: Present-perfect passive with tense-change distractors; CGL voice style

questions.question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.
She said to me, "I will help you tomorrow."
options: She told me that I will help you tomorrow.
She told me that she would help me the next day.
She said to me that she will help me the next day.
She told me that she would help you tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'Said to' → 'told'; 'will' → 'would'; 'I' → 'she', 'you' → 'me'; 'tomorrow' → 'the next day'.

relevance.note: Will→would, tomorrow→next day indirect speech; CGL narration standard

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Mangrove forests grow along tropical coastlines where land meets the sea. Their tangled roots slow down incoming waves and trap sediment, which helps protect the shore from erosion and storm surges. These forests also serve as nurseries for many species of fish and crabs, supporting the livelihoods of coastal communities. Yet mangroves have been cleared at an alarming rate for shrimp farms, ports and housing. Scientists point out that a hectare of mangrove can store several times more carbon than a hectare of many inland forests, because most of the carbon is locked in waterlogged soil where it decays very slowly. Restoring mangroves is therefore seen not merely as a conservation measure but as a practical defence against climate change.

According to the passage, how do mangroves protect the shoreline?
options: They raise the level of the land every year
They stop rainfall from reaching the coast
They prevent fishermen from going to sea
Their roots slow down waves and trap sediment
questions.explanation: The passage says their tangled roots slow incoming waves and trap sediment, protecting the shore from erosion and storm surges.

relevance.note: Factual RC on mangroves; matches CGL passage questions

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Mangrove forests grow along tropical coastlines where land meets the sea. Their tangled roots slow down incoming waves and trap sediment, which helps protect the shore from erosion and storm surges. These forests also serve as nurseries for many species of fish and crabs, supporting the livelihoods of coastal communities. Yet mangroves have been cleared at an alarming rate for shrimp farms, ports and housing. Scientists point out that a hectare of mangrove can store several times more carbon than a hectare of many inland forests, because most of the carbon is locked in waterlogged soil where it decays very slowly. Restoring mangroves is therefore seen not merely as a conservation measure but as a practical defence against climate change.

Why can mangroves store more carbon than many inland forests?
options: Most of their carbon is held in waterlogged soil where it decays very slowly
Mangrove trees are much taller than inland trees
Mangroves grow only in cold regions
Shrimp farms add carbon to mangrove soil
questions.explanation: The passage states that most of the carbon is locked in waterlogged soil where it decays very slowly.

relevance.note: Reason-based factual RC; CGL style

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Mangrove forests grow along tropical coastlines where land meets the sea. Their tangled roots slow down incoming waves and trap sediment, which helps protect the shore from erosion and storm surges. These forests also serve as nurseries for many species of fish and crabs, supporting the livelihoods of coastal communities. questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island. Concrete, asphalt and brick absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly after sunset, so city nights remain uncomfortably warm. Tall buildings trap this heat further by blocking the breeze, while the steady stream of vehicles and air-conditioners adds waste heat of its own. The consequences are not trivial: higher night temperatures increase electricity demand, worsen air quality and pose a serious risk to the elderly and to outdoor workers. Planners, however, have discovered that the problem can be eased with modest measures. Trees and parks cool their surroundings by providing shade and releasing moisture, and roofs painted in light colours reflect much of the sunlight that would otherwise be absorbed. Some cities now require new buildings to include green roofs. None of these steps can make a city as cool as a village, but together they can make urban summers far more bearable.

According to the passage, why do city nights remain warm?
options: Building materials release the heat they stored during the day
Villages send warm winds into cities at night
questions.explanation: The passage says concrete, asphalt and brick absorb sunlight by day and release the stored heat slowly after sunset.

relevance.note: Factual RC urban heat island; CGL passage
